152151 --  until it fails.

351350 --    string.

360359 --  - If at least one of `re₁` and `re₂` matches `s`, then
361360 --    `Union re₁ re₂` matches `s`.
362---

363362 --  - Finally, if we can write some string `s` as the
364363 --    concatenation of a sequence of strings
365364 --    `s = s₁ ++ ... ++ sₖ`, and the expression `re` matches
366365 --    each one of the strings `sᵢ`, then `Star re` matches
367366 --    `s`.
368---
367+
369368 --    In particular, the sequence of strings may be empty,
370369 --    so `Star re` always matches the empty string `[]` no

128126 --  Fortunately, there is another way to do it: We can
129127 --  express the concept "reaches `1` eventually in the
130128 --  Collatz sequence" as an *inductively defined property*
131129 --  of numbers. Intuitively, this property is defined by a
132130 --  set of rules:
133---

135---                     CollatzHoldsFor 1
136---
137---      even n = true     CollatzHoldsFor (div2 n)
138---      ─────────────────────────────────────────── (chf_even)
139---                     CollatzHoldsFor n
140---
141---      even n = false    CollatzHoldsFor ((3 * n) + 1)
142---      ─────────────────────────────────────────────── (chf_odd)
143---                     CollatzHoldsFor n

672625 --  What does it mean to say that "an element `x` occurs in
673626 --  a list `l`"?
674---
627+
675628 --  - If `l` is the empty list, then `x` cannot occur in it,
676629 --    so the property "`x` appears in `l`" is simply false.
677---
630+

679632 --    case, `x` occurs in `l` if it is equal to `x'` or if
680633 --    it occurs in `l'`.

752703 --  derivation establishing the truth of the statement
753704 --  `∀ n m : Nat, n + m = m + n`. The type of this object is
754705 --  the proposition that it is a proof of.

762713 --    can use that theorem for.

210210 --  whenever possible, computation should be *pure*, in the
211211 --  sense that the only effect of execution should be to
217217 --  order, a pure sorting function would take the original
218218 --  list and return a fresh list containing the same numbers
219219 --  in sorted order.

229229 --  reasoning about concurrent systems, where every piece of
230230 --  mutable state shared between threads is a potential
231231 --  source of pernicious bugs.

294---  #### Downloading and using the book for a class
295-
296---  If you are **using this book as part of a class**, your
297---  instructor will have created a "student" release for
298---  you. Download the `.zip` file for that release, unzip
299---  it, and then open the resulting directory in VS Code.
300---  Open any `.lean` file (e.g., `LF/Basics.lean`) to get
301---  started.
302---
303---  If you would like to read the HTML version of the book,
304---  it should be hosted on your course website (you may be
305---  reading it now!).
306---
307---  Note that, as the book is changing while you are taking
308---  your class, you should download a fresh `.zip` for each
309---  homework you do, opening it in a fresh directory. This
310---  way you will have access to prior solutions, and you
311---  will automatically get any Lean updates. More on
312---  exercises below.
313-
314---  #### Downloading and building the book from Git, for self study
315-
316---  If you are **reading Software Foundations on your own**,
317---  you can get the most up-to-date version from the
318---  [SF-in-Lean](https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean)
319---  GitHub repository. Clone that repository and then build
320---  it by typing `make lf-student` from the root directory.
321---  Doing so will construct the student version (full prose,
322---  with solutions elided) of the *Logical Foundations*
323---  book.
324---
325---  Building the book requires that you have Lean installed.
326---  If you do not, follow the instructions
327---  [here](https://lean-lang.org/install/manual/) to install
328---  the Lean toolchain manager `elan` which will then manage
329---  your Lean installation. Alternatively, once you have
330---  added the Lean 4 extension to VS Code, you can open a
331---  Lean file in the repository (for example, `LF.lean` from
332---  the top level directory) and it will install `elan` and
333---  Lean automatically. Both installation methods have the
334---  same effect, putting the Lean toolchain in the same
335---  place on your filesystem.
336---
337---  With Lean installed, `make lf-student` writes two things
338---  to `_out/lf/student/`:
339---
340---  - `html/`, an HTML-formatted version of the whole book;
341---    and
342---
343---  - `lean/`, a standalone Lean project holding the same
344---    chapters as `.lean` files, with solutions to exercises
345---    omitted.
346---
347---  Use `make student` instead if you also want *Type
348---  Systems* (`ts`) and *Hoare Logic* (`hl`). The first
349---  build compiles the whole dependency tree and takes a
350---  while; later builds are incremental.
351---
352---  Now you can open the generated Lean project as its own
353---  folder — not as a file inside your clone:
354---
355---      code _out/lf/student/lean
356---
357---  or
358---
359---      cd _out/lf/student/lean
360---      code .
361---
362---  You can also use File → Open Folder.
363---
364---  Treat this as a scratch copy: **every `make` regenerates
365---  it from the Verso sources, overwriting whatever is
366---  there.** Work on your proofs here, but keep anything you
367---  want to survive somewhere else.
368---
369---  If you would like to read the book HTML, start a local
370---  HTTP server and point it at the generated HTML files:
371---
372---      python3 -m http.server 8000 -d _out/lf/student/html
373---
374---  Then visit `http://localhost:8000` and start reading.
375---
376---  If you want to build everything — student version,
377---  "terse" instructor version, solutions, and grading
378---  versions — type `make`, `make lf`, etc.

410405 --  interact. As a simple example, let's use a typeclass to
411406 --  define a *monoid*, a simple algebraic structure that
412407 --  includes four things:
413---
408+
414409 --  - an underlying set of data, represented by a type `α`,
415---
410+
416411 --  - an operator (which we'll write `⊗`, typed otimes) that
417412 --    combines two elements of type `α` into one,
418---
413+
419414 --  - a particular element `id` of type `α`, which we call
420415 --    the "identity element", and
421---
416+
422417 --  - some laws about the interaction of `⊗` and `id`,
423418 --    namely that:
424---
419+
425420 --    - `∀ x, id ⊗ x = x = x ⊗ id`, and
426---
421+
427422 --    - `∀ x y z, x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z` (i.e., that `⊗`
428423 --      is associative)
429---
424+
430425 --  We can express these requirements in the form of a
431426 --  typeclass:
432427 
438433 
439434 class Monoid (α : Type) extends (OpSet α) where
440435   id : α
441-  left_id  (x : α)  : id ⊗ x = x
442-  right_id (x : α)  : x ⊗ id = x
443-  assoc (x y z : α) : x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z
436+  left_id : ∀ (x : α), id ⊗ x = x
437+  right_id : ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ id = x
438+  assoc : ∀ (x y z : α), x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z
444439 
445440 --  The `extends` keyword indicates that the `Monoid`
446441 --  typeclass extends the `OpSet` typeclass, which just

449444 --  similar to how a class would in an object-oriented
